sections.h2: What to do first when selling in Warrington
sections.html:
Warrington Township makes the seller get an Occupancy Certificate before settlement. In practice that means applying at least 30 days ahead, paying $140 for each residential unit and passing a township inspection. The duty sits with the seller or landlord, though a real estate agent or other representative can file for you. After that, the sale runs through Pennsylvania's usual disclosure, tax and recording steps.

The township has about 26,261 residents in 9,605 households, and 81.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. The midpoint home value is $553,100, and household income at the midpoint is $133,179. Many houses were built from the 1980s through the 2000s, when the population climbed from 10,704 to 23,418. Few people move out in a given year, since 92.5 percent were in the same house a year earlier, so buyers are often families moving for the Central Bucks School District. A clean inspection result and a certificate in hand carry real weight with them.

The certificate is a township inspection confirming that a home meets safety and property maintenance standards before it changes hands. The Permits Office accepts applications online, by mail or in person at the township building. Whoever applies must make sure the fee is paid and the inspection is booked.

Warrington occupancy certificate terms
RequirementAmount or timing
When to applyAt least 30 days before settlement
Residential fee$140 per unit
How long a certificate lasts60 days from the date issued
Fire sprinkler certification, where a system existsValid for six months
  • Commercial fees differ, so confirm the amount before you submit.
  • A house with a fire sprinkler system needs its own inspection and certification from a registered third-party agency.
  • The township posts a residential inspection checklist. Walk the house with it before the inspector does and fix the cheap items first.

Because a certificate lasts only 60 days, do not schedule the inspection months ahead of closing. If a deal collapses and the certificate lapses, the next buyer means a new application. Count that risk into your timeline if your buyer needs a loan.

sections.h2: Sprinkler systems and other special cases
sections.html:
A sprinkler system adds a step. A registered third-party agency has to inspect and certify it before the occupancy certificate can be issued, and the township keeps a list of registered agencies. Book that visit early, since it runs separately from the township's own inspection.

Landlords selling a rental face the same certificate rule. Since the duty falls on the seller or landlord, a tenant-occupied house still needs the certificate before settlement, so arrange access dates with the tenant when you set the inspection.

Two percent of the value is the total transfer tax on a Bucks County sale: 1 percent for the state, 1 percent shared by the municipality and school district. The recorder collects it as the deed goes on file. Expect to be turned away if you offer a personal check. Cash at the counter, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card all work.

Who pays is a matter for your contract, and splitting it is common. Family transfers can qualify for an exemption. If the deed does not spell that out, include a Statement of Value form with it.

The seller's disclosure duty comes from 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. You hand the buyer a signed statement before the agreement of sale is signed, covering the roof, basement, drainage, plumbing, wiring and similar items. Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information, which is relevant in a township with several creeks.

Assessment appeals go to the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals, and a change from an annual appeal applies to the following tax year. Call the Board for the current filing deadline. The homestead and farmstead exclusion filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1. A new owner must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of buying, so remind your buyer.

sections.h2: Creeks, drainage and what buyers ask
sections.html:
Warrington has the Little Neshaminy Creek, Mill Creek and Park Creek running through it, and buyers compare houses on drainage as much as on drive time. Expect questions about the basement and the roof. Have dates for any roof work, receipts for sump or waterproofing repairs, and any insurance claim history ready to hand over.

If a buyer asks about development nearby, send them to the township's Planning and Zoning staff, who work with the Bucks County Planning Commission on zoning updates. Keep your own survey and permit records in the closing file as well.

The checklist is the best preview you will get. Print it, then go room by room and exterior by exterior, marking anything that looks like it would fail. Small fixes done before the inspector arrives are cheaper than a failed visit and a second appointment, and a repeat visit can push you past the 60-day window of a certificate you were hoping to use.

If the inspection turns up larger problems, you have the usual choices. Repair them yourself, negotiate a credit with a buyer who will do the work, or sell to a buyer who agrees in writing to handle the certificate items. Whichever way you go, get the responsibility for each item written into the contract.

sections.h2: Fix it, list it or sell as-is?
sections.html:
High values reward a house that shows well. Even so, the 30-day lead time for the certificate and any sprinkler certification can slow a rushed listing. A cash buyer taking the house as-is still needs the township certificate handled before settlement, so ask how that will work before you agree to a date.

  • Apply for the certificate as soon as you have a contract, not at the closing table.
  • Go through the township checklist yourself and fix inexpensive items first.
  • Compare a listing net sheet with a cash offer that says who pays for any repair the inspector requires.

After you accept an offer, sequence matters more than speed. First, file the occupancy certificate application, since the 30-day lead time is the longest fixed step. Second, line up the sprinkler certification if your house has a system. Third, request payoff figures for any mortgage from your lender. Fourth, sign the disclosure statement if it is not already part of the contract package.

At settlement the deed is signed and recorded, the transfer tax is paid, and the payoff is taken from your proceeds. Keep the certificate, the checklist results and any repair receipts together so the buyer's agent can see them at once. With a cash buyer there is no appraisal or loan approval, which leaves the township certificate and the title work as the only things between you and a closing date.

faqs.q: How much is the occupancy certificate in Warrington?
faqs.a: The township charges $140 per unit for residential properties. Commercial fees differ, so confirm the amount before you submit.

faqs.q: How long does a Warrington occupancy certificate last?
faqs.a: It is valid for 60 days from the date issued. If settlement slips past that window, you will need a new certificate.

faqs.q: Who applies for the certificate when a house is sold?
faqs.a: The seller or landlord is responsible, and an agent or authorized representative can file for the seller. The certificate has to be in hand before settlement.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Warrington?
faqs.a: Owners report a midpoint value of $553,100 for 2020 to 2024. Your own price still depends on condition and recent nearby sales.

faqs.q: Does my sprinkler system change anything?
faqs.a: Yes. A house with fire sprinklers needs a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency before the occupancy certificate can be issued. That sprinkler certification lasts six months, and the township posts a list of registered agencies.
